Nestle Denies California Bottled Water Factories Contribute To Drought

That is because it really doesn't.

Anyone that cares to look at the math can see where the largest percentage of water is going to. And it sure as fuck isn't bottled water.

Irrigation: 60.7% (23,056 million gallons per day)

Thermoelectric power generation: 17.4% (6,601 million gallons per day)

Public supply: 16.6% (6,307 million gallons per day). Average daily gross per capita use was 181 gallons (total Public Supply withdrawals divided by population served).

Aquaculture: 2.6% (973 million gallons per day)

Industrial: 1.0% (400 million gallons per day)

Mining: 0.7% (272 million gallons per day)

Livestock: 0.5% (188 million gallons per day)

Self-supply domestic: 0.5% (172 million gallons per day). Average daily per capita use was 69 gallons.

According to Nestle(and no one has proposed alternative numbers that I could find), they used 703 million gallons of water last year. If you go back and look at the other statistics, those are PER DAY.

In short, they are not contributing to the drought. Shitty water management from the state is contributing to the drought.

In the late 90's I got into making levels for Unreal, then got into the Unreal community forum. When Unreal Tournament launched the community was large and solid, lots of amazing people. Over time the community thinned but the core people stayed on. The forum changed hands and was run by GT Interactive, but was still the UT forums. There was a major falling out and GT screwed the forums and all the core members moved to a "Refugee Camp" so we were the GTFRC (GT Forums, Refugee Camp).

The best people I've ever met were in that crew.

The guy who made the "All Your Base" animation/video was there. We had such an awesome group of people. Think I chatted with them for about 13 years or so. It was awesome watching people's lives grow and mature. I was a member from the time I was in highschool till after I got married and had my first kid. Its kind of amazing thinking about watching each other grow up.

There was no one point that I can point to and say "That was the best part!" but the time and group as a whole was simply amazing. We watched the internet grow up together.

I used to post on many forums and extensively used MSN back when I was a kid. Back then, the internet used to be a fun place to explore.

Ahh, the good old days. You see, I lived in the country for much of my teenage years, so first it was Dial-up in a post Dial-up world (2005-2008). I was 13-14 at the time and many days and nights were spent looking for Sims 2 mods on various sites (mostly MTS2) and then waiting for them to download, sometimes hours at a time. I had a 1MB/file limit to what I was supposed to be allowed to download, but I regularly pushed that further. I learned what downloads were smaller (textures, lots) and which were larger (new objects, neighborhoods) quickly. I also found my first piece of go-to software, which I still use today: 7-zip to mass unzip the files I downloaded.

Then, when I got my first "laptop" (which was a hulking HP dinosaur with a burnt out power board, meaning I had to use a giant-ass docking station) I discovered my neighbor's Wifi. I still have no clue what kind of internet they had back then (it was probably either DSL or satellite), nor which neighbor it who it actually came from, but I remember spending many nights either on our front porch or in my bed sitting just right to steal the wifi so I could get on without my parents having to log me on. They knew I was on the internet, but not what I was doing; it was my first taste of freedom.

I also got into emulation at the time, which was incredible because I had many good memories of playing old games before my dad bastardized our SNES power cord for use in our van. Many, many days and nights were spent getting old game, mods, and other things. I even remember my first act of contemporary piracy: downloading a Japanese Pokemon Diamond ROM over eMule. I didn't even know what p2p was at the time, nor where to find pirated material beyond older ROMs, but I managed through sheer tenacity to find an eMule download of this ROM because I was sick of waiting for it to come out in the US. Needless to say I was quite disappointed when no$GBA didn't play it yet...

Fast forward a few years and we moved into a different place still in the country. We moved on up to cellular internet, which was a bit faster, but was still on 2G where we lived, so not much. It was frustrating because the line for high speed internet was a few hundred feet down the road from the trailer park. The card was also only compatible with my dad's laptop, so there was little privacy to be had, but I knew private browsing well enough to use at night. It was at that time when I found my first internet forums: some old retro gaming ones in particular.

I remember my excitement when my father bought a video card for our desktop that we had (I still have that, along with the old HP dinosaur packed away) because it meant that I could play games on PC again. I eventually got Oblivion GOTY on the advice of the guy working the Movie Gallery counter, and it was the first non-Sims game I put serious time into, both with modding and playing. It is the game that made me truly love PC over console even though I already had a PS3 and Wii at the time. It was also one of my first Mature games (both in tone and rating) the other being the Metal Gear Solid series.

I'm already rambling here so I should wrap this up. It's late here and I need to get more work done tonight.
The one thing I noticed in your post was saying that MGS was your first mature game, meaning you must have had been lucky enough to get Oblivion when it was rated T.

Nah, I played Oblivion about a year after picking up the MGS collection for PS2. It was re-rated long before it came to PS3 anyway and I didn't have a 360 and the time. They were still the first two (well 4 including all the MGS games from the set) big M rated games I got for myself though, so both series holds a special place for me. Up to that point I either sneaked them from my brother or played at friends' houses, but these were the first two I actually could sit down and play without sneaking around.

I wish I would have known about the controversy at the time though, it would've been much easier to convince my mother to let me get Oblivion.
